key_concept: Solubility cannot be ranked from $K_{sp}$ alone when salts have different ion stoichiometry; convert each $K_{sp}$ to molar solubility $s$ ($K_{sp}=s^2$ for AB and $K_{sp}=4s^3$ for AB$_2$) and then compare $s$.
steps: $AgBr \rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + Br^-$ is an AB type salt, so $K_{sp}=s^2$. This gives $s=\sqrt{5.0\times10^{-13}}\approx 7.07\times10^{-7}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

$Zn(OH)_2 \rightleftharpoons Zn^{2+} + 2OH^-$ is an AB$_2$ type salt, so $K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3$. This gives $s^3=\dfrac{1.0\times10^{-15}}{4}=2.5\times10^{-16}$, so $s\approx 6.3\times10^{-6}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Mercury(I) exists as the dimer $Hg_2^{2+}$, so $Hg_2Cl_2 \rightleftharpoons Hg_2^{2+} + 2Cl^-$ and $K_{sp}=4s^3$. This gives $s^3=\dfrac{1.3\times10^{-18}}{4}=3.25\times10^{-19}$, so $s\approx 6.9\times10^{-7}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.
So the order of solubility is $Zn(OH)_2 > AgBr > Hg_2Cl_2$.
why_not_others: Option (2) follows the raw $K_{sp}$ values, but $Zn(OH)_2$ is an AB$_2$ salt, so its solubility ($\sim10^{-6}$ M) exceeds that of $AgBr$ ($\sim10^{-7}$ M). Options (1) and (3) wrongly put $Hg_2Cl_2$ on top, although it has the lowest molar solubility.
common_trap: Students either rank the salts directly by $K_{sp}$, or write mercurous chloride as $2Hg^+ + 2Cl^-$ instead of $Hg_2^{2+} + 2Cl^-$, which gives a wrong, much larger solubility.
time_saving_tip: Estimate $s\approx\sqrt[3]{K_{sp}/4}$ only for the AB$_2$ salts. $Zn(OH)_2$ comes out near $6\times10^{-6}$, clearly the highest, which already eliminates options (1), (2) and (3).
